items.title: A.B. Spellman interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 19, 2022
items.q: Louis Armstrong for example, was a voice for the ages. I mean I don’t think he will ever be obsolete.

ctx.x: Years ago I went, it might have been the same jazz educators’ gathering that you were at. There was a panel about, that was entitled “Trad Jazz Is Alive and Well” and it had some record label people and some players. But on the program for the three or four days there was no trad jazz groups that performed. I started thinking about jazz in the larger sense has been elevated to a high art form and it’s in the universities and it is studied and you can get Ph.D.s in it but is New Orleans music and trad jazz and…

I don’t think a lot of people listen to New Orleans music anymore. It’s too bad because it’s still great music. There was a lot of brilliance in the 1920s and coming forward. And it still speaks, at least to me today. Louis Armstrong for example, was a voice for the © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

ages. I mean I don’t think he will ever be obsolete. But still I think most people know Louis from the singing he did say during the 1950s to the end of his life than they do from the times when he was breaking through and establishing himself as the future of music. And there was one — Charles — what is his name — one of the great white Civil Rights lawyers had written about how he grew up in Texas in a world of segregation and had assumed all of the things that go with segregation and Jim Crow about…
